title: Large-Scale Web Applications
author: Mendel Rosenblum · Stanford CS142
scope: This demo checks selected learning objectives from slides 4–10 of the 22-slide English lecture. Other slides remain readable in the PDF but are not assessed. Source passages below are verbatim excerpts with whitespace normalized; concept descriptions and questions are Hearo-authored learning aids. The original PDF is linked, not republished.

referenceLines.text: Expand capacity by adding more instances
Scale-up architecture - Switch to a bigger instance
Challenge: Need to manage multiple instances and distribute work to them
Use load balancing to distribute incoming HTTP requests across many front-end web servers
Load balancer directs TCP connection request to one of the many web servers
Load balancer will send all packets for that connection to the same server.
Can select web server based on random or on load estimates
Fault tolerant - web server dies the load balance just quits using it
Stateless servers make load balancing easier
Different requests from the same user can be handled by different servers
Requires database to be shared across web servers
WebSockets bind browsers and web server
Data sharding - Spread database over scale-out instances
Each piece is called data shard
Can tolerate failures by replication - place more than one copy of data (3 is common)
Applications must partition data among multiple independent databases, which adds complexity.
Key-value store (both keys and values are arbitrary blobs)
Used to cache results of recent database queries
Writes must still go to the DBMS, so no performance improvement for them
Cache misses still hurt performance
Must manage consistency in software (e.g., flush relevant memcache data when database gets modified)

concepts.label: Scale out vs. scale up
concepts.description: Distinguish adding instances from using a bigger instance, including the work-distribution challenge.
concepts.question: How does adding instances differ from switching to a bigger instance?

concepts.label: Load balancing
concepts.description: Explain distributing incoming requests across web servers and handling a failed server.
concepts.question: How are requests distributed, and what happens when a web server fails?

concepts.label: Stateless servers
concepts.description: Explain why requests from one user can reach different servers and why a shared database matters.
concepts.question: Why do stateless servers make load balancing easier?

concepts.label: Data sharding
concepts.description: Explain partitioning data across database instances and the added application complexity.
concepts.question: What is split when data is sharded, and what complexity does that add?

concepts.label: Replication
concepts.description: Explain keeping more than one copy of data to tolerate failures. Advanced replication and backups are outside this source scope.
concepts.question: How can keeping multiple copies of data help tolerate failures?

concepts.label: Caching and consistency
concepts.description: Explain caching query results, cache misses, writes to the database, and software-managed consistency.
concepts.question: If the database changes, why might the cached result need to be removed or updated?
